name: LZMA (7-Zip LZMA SDK)
workload: lzbench 2.4, in-memory, single thread, silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes): compress speed, decompress speed and output size of lzma 26.03 (the 7-Zip LZMA code as built in lzbench) against bzip2 1.0.8 at several levels.
claimed_speedup: lzma 26.03 -9: 2.55 MB/s compress, 78.2 MB/s decompress, 48,682,482 bytes (22.97%); bzip2 1.0.8 -9: 12.7 MB/s compress, 35.5 MB/s decompress, 54,572,811 bytes (25.75%). Decompression about 2.2x faster with 10.8% smaller output, but compression about 5.0x slower (derived from page data). At matching output size: lzma 26.03 -0 29.5 / 62.3 MB/s, 60,520,844 bytes (28.55%) against bzip2 1.0.8 -1 13.5 / 41.1 MB/s, 60,484,813 bytes (28.54%): about 2.2x faster compress and 1.5x faster decompress (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary), lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; the public lzbench Makefile builds everything at -O3 -DNDEBUG except codecs that set O2
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P @ 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
stars_or_usage: ip7z/7zip GitHub repo 4.1k stars; 7-Zip 26.04 released 2026-10-06 (7,243 weekly SourceForge downloads); LZMA/LZMA2 are the default methods of the 7z and xz formats
tradeoffs: LZ77 plus range coder aimed at maximum ratio with small decoder memory (lzma.txt: 'maximum increasing of compression ratio, keeping high decompression speed and low memory requirements for decompressing'). Compression is slow (2.55 MB/s at -9 on one thread). Decompression is about twice bzip2's but about a quarter of zlib's: zlib 1.3.2 -9 decodes at 318 MB/s against 78.2 MB/s, so LZMA trades roughly 4x slower decoding for a 28% smaller file than zlib -9 (22.97% against 31.92%, derived from page data). The ANSI-C decoder (C/LzmaDec.c) is small and portable; the SDK encoder is C as well (C/LzmaEnc.c).
caveats: The 7-Zip project makes no numeric speed claim for LZMA: DOC/lzma.txt only says LZMA keeps 'high decompression speed and low memory requirements' and compares to nothing; the numbers come from the third-party lzbench README, which also shows the LZMA SDK code losing to xz 5.8.4 on both speeds at about the same size (xz -9: 2.75 MB/s compress, 122 MB/s decompress, 23.01%, against lzma -9: 2.55 / 78.2 MB/s, 22.97%), so the win is against bzip2 only and the baseline is not the strongest LZMA implementation; zstd 1.5.7 -18 (4.13 MB/s compress, 1175 MB/s decompress, 25.14%) and brotli 1.2.0 -11 (0.56 / 383 MB/s, 23.78%) decode far faster. The lzbench 'lzma' row is the 7-Zip LZMA code compiled by lzbench with its own flags, not a 7-Zip release binary; one corpus (silesia.tar), one machine. Compression is 5x slower than bzip2 -9 in the same table. The sourceforge.net/projects/sevenzip/files/7-Zip page (opened) shows releases only (26.04 on 2026-10-06) and no licence; www.7-zip.org and the SDK pages are blocked here. The ip7z/7zip GitHub repo is the source home linked by name in its README ('7-Zip on GitHub', pointing to 7-zip.org) but its page did not confirm it as the official mirror, and its last commit date was not shown (last_commit null). Licence: DOC/readme.txt says the LZMA SDK 'is written and placed in the public domain by Igor Pavlov' (no patent grant); the rest of 7-Zip is GNU LGPL with some BSD 3-clause code and an unRAR licence restriction, so copy only the LZMA SDK files (C/LzmaDec.c, C/LzmaEnc.c and friends) under the public-domain dedication.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://sourceforge.net/projects/sevenzip/files/7-Zip (listed in fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Compression as the default and general compression method of the 7z format); numbers from the lzbench 2.4 README, source from github.com/ip7z/7zip
